When your audio input is amplified, the input isn't made bigger (as if your input was stretched like silly putty to become bigger). Instead, the weaker input is used to another electrical input. A small change in the input, causes a larger swing in the "amplified" output.

A tube (or a transistor which works pretty much the same) becomes an amplifier because its grid modulates the current flow between the cathode and plate.

That is to say, a 1 watt current on the grid, really its voltage is important in this case, causes the 260 watts flowing between cathode and plate to duplicate the modulation of the weaker grid signal. Bear in mind the meaning of modulation which is the frequency and amplitude that creates sound, radio waves, light, whatever we're talking about. So a 1 watt signal controls the amplitude and frequency of the full-power signal (not exactly but close enough for this explanation).

The high-power comes from the amplifier's power supply, usually a transformer that matches house current to whatever the designers need for the tube to work. Tubes can be made to run on low voltage or high voltage, cool temperatures or very high temperatures but usually they need ~ 1000 volts AC and are very hot since the cathodes must be very hot, like the filament in a lamp, to work properly.

Transistors function much like tubes but they're so small the power requirements are a fraction of vacuum tubes and they can be made almost infinitely tiny on integrated circuits.

Many people prefer the sound coming from a tube amplifier to the sound from a transistorized amplifier. In theory it shouldn't matter but in fact vacuum tubes and transistors do have characteristic "sounds" and tubes are, to my trained musician's ears, warmer.in their output -- more pleasant to hear, without the harshness of solid state. It's the same debate as analog LPs/tape versus digital.

The thing about tubes is they're made like lightbulbs so they can break easily and can slowly leak ruining the vacuum. But they're also more resistant to electrical abuse than solid state devices so people like them for heavy-duty use so long as they're built into a strong chassis and you've got spares on hand!
